title: I Took the Community Pizza-Oven Peel Log to the Host Who Left My Dough on the Stone

parts.text: I opened the oven door at 5:06 p.m. and host Brice was already launching over my numbered dough. The slate said: ONE STONE. FORTY MINUTES. PEEL STAYS WITH THE BOOKING. I was thirty-six, kitchen volunteer, holding a flour ticket that listed our lot. Brice shrugged. "Hosts are the fire." I photographed the slate, the booking, and his pie on my stone. Then I asked for the peel log. At 5:14 the kitchen pinged why Brice's name was on my peel. I kept my voice oven-quiet and let the timestamp talk. A slate is only a slate until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The kitchen can see Brice's pie on my stone during our booking.

social.video_title: He launched over my numbered dough on my stone — Part 1/2
social.description: Pizza oven, a host on my stone, a forty-minute clock he posted. I logged the launch. Would you have asked for the peel log?

parts.text: Brice called it a heat-check until the kitchen asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the slate, and the pie still. The peel went back to my handle. Brice ran his own forty and told the next host atmosphere was always about crust. Crust is a word hosts use when a booking exists. Stone policy now has a second line: HOSTS ARE NOT THE FIRE. I keep our peel on a labeled rack. Brice brown-bags his jokes. The oven finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.description: Peel log, numbered dough, and a second line on the slate. Was a heat-check ever my stone?
